name: Tanning oil

lead: Tanning oils are cosmetic oils applied to skin in the sun to deepen colour and give a glossy bronzed finish. Jean Patou's 1927 product is described as the first, and baby oil was common in the 1950s.

The chain is cosmetic: sun-exposure oils do not themselves darken skin, since tanning comes from UV acting on melanocytes, but they add sheen to the result. A newer category blends oils with DHA, which colours the dead outer skin layer through a browning reaction without UV. No clinical trials of tanning oils for appearance were found.

paras: People apply the oil before or during sunbathing, or choose a DHA-based oil to build colour without sun. Many pair it with sun exposure for a glossy finish.
Sunburn is the most common UV hazard, and excess exposure raises skin cancer risk. Oils with low or no SPF offer little protection, and DHA colour does not protect from UV.

angle.text: You apply tanning oil while sunbathing to deepen colour and give skin a glossy bronzed finish. The tan comes from sun exposure, and oils have been used for this since the 1920s. Sunless DHA oils give colour without UV.

lead: Tanning oil is a cosmetic oil applied to the skin while sunbathing, traditionally intended to encourage a deeper, glossier tan. People use it to get a darker, bronzed look, and some sunless versions add colour without UV. Wikipedia credits Jean Patou's 1927 'Huile de Chaldee' as the first sun tan oil and notes baby oil was widely used in the 1950s to increase tanning.[1]

The oil itself does not darken skin: tanning arises from UV acting on melanocytes, while the oil is described as giving sheen and, depending on formulation, little or no sun protection.[1] Product patents also describe sunless oil-in-water emulsions combining DHA with vegetable oils, and sunless tanners based on DHA tint the skin's outer layer without UV.[2][3][4]

Tanned skin was a marker of outdoor labour before the 1920s and became fashionable after Coco Chanel returned from the French Riviera with a tan; tanning oils, then tanning beds from 1978, grew up alongside that fashion.[1][5] Health bodies have since reported that UV exposure raises skin-cancer risk, and sunless products developed in parallel as a way to a bronzed look without UV.[1][5][2]
No clinical trials of tanning oils as appearance products were located. Sunscreen availability has been examined in a cross-sectional US study, which is not specific to tanning oils.[6]
infobox: Sun oils; indoor-tanning lotions; DHA self-tanning oils

paras: Sun tanning oils are applied to exposed skin during sunbathing and may contain low SPF or none.[1] DHA oils are a separate sunless type, described in patent filings as emulsions of DHA with a vegetable oil containing C18 unsaturated fatty acids.[3][4] Another patent describes light-protection formulations with DHA.[7]

Wikipedia's indoor tanning lotion article describes related products meant for use with tanning beds, including accelerators that are said to promote melanin production, bronzers that give an immediate darker colour, and 'tingle' lotions with ingredients that increase blood flow or cause a tingling sensation. Listed ingredients include L-tyrosine, tea oil, copper compounds, green tea extract and natural oils such as hempseed. Most indoor lotions have no SPF, though many now include it, and mineral oil in some baby oils can damage acrylic bed shields.[8]

Natural tanning arises from melanocytes making melanin after UV exposure; UVB-induced melanin appears two to three days later and provides a modest SPF of about 3.[1] DHA reacts with amino acids in the dead outer skin layer and does not use melanin or UV; the colour lasts roughly 3 to 10 days.[2] Wikipedia says DHA is not a dye, stain or paint, and that DHA products usually contain 3 to 5 percent DHA, adjusted for lighter or darker shades.[2]

Tan accelerators, usually containing tyrosine and used with UV exposure, are the subject of claims that Wikipedia says lack supporting scientific data.[2] Bronzers of cosmetic, natural or DHA type wash off or fade over about 1 to 5 days depending on type.[8]

Before the 1920s tanned skin signalled outdoor labour; after Coco Chanel returned from the French Riviera with a tan it became fashionable, and Patou's oil appeared in 1927.[1] SPF ratings began in 1962.[1] On the sunless side, Eva Wittgenstein found in the 1950s that DHA stained skin brown; Man-Tan came out in 1959 and Coppertone's QT in 1960, both giving orange-toned results.[2]

Other milestones in the fashion for tanning include the 1946 debut of the bikini, 1950s sunbathing advertising and Coppertone's 1953 ad, the 1975 invention of the sunbed by Friedrich Wolff, and the first US sales of his devices in 1978.[1][5] From the late 1990s, automated spray-tan booths broadened the sunless market.[2]

Bronzers are wash-off products in powder, spray, mousse, gel and lotion forms that give an immediate colour; the term is not legally defined, and the FDA regulates DHA as the colour additive in such products. Some can leave rub-off on clothing or look orange or patchy if misapplied.[2]

Tanning pills based on carotenoids such as canthaxanthin can change skin colour from the inside; the FDA has not approved beta-carotene or canthaxanthin for tanning, and the agency has an import alert covering oral tanning tablets.[2] Psoralen-based tanning activators were banned by health authorities in July 1996 because they are photocarcinogenic.[1]
No studies found. A US cross-sectional study of sunscreen availability in three counties examined sunscreen products generally, not tanning oils.[6]

The FDA states that tanning beds and booths are regulated as radiation-emitting devices rather than cosmetics, sunscreens are regulated as drugs, and tanning products regulated as cosmetics carry a required warning statement when they contain no sunscreen. Sunscreens began receiving SPF ratings in 1962, and SPF 15 products and standardised US labelling appeared in 1978.[1]

For indoor tanning, the WHO classifies UV radiation as a Group 1 carcinogen following a 2009 IARC review. Several countries bar minors from tanning beds (France was first, in 1997), Brazil banned cosmetic tanning-bed use in 2009, Australia banned commercial tanning services in 2015, and in 2014 the FDA moved tanning beds from low-risk to moderate-risk devices with a black-box warning for under-18s.[5]

Sunburn is the most frequent UV hazard, and excessive exposure is associated with skin ageing and skin cancer.[1] Products without sunscreen offer less protection. For about 24 hours after DHA application, skin is reported to be more susceptible to free-radical damage from sunlight, DHA and erythrulose can cause contact dermatitis in some people, and the FDA approves DHA only for external use, not around the eyes, lips or mucous membranes or for inhalation.[2] Sunscreens built into self-tanners lose effectiveness quickly, according to Wikipedia.[2]

Wikipedia's article on indoor tanning cites a 2012 review finding a 20% higher melanoma risk for anyone who had used a tanning device (59% higher for starting before age 35), and a 2014 meta-analysis finding a 16% higher risk, rising to 35% for those starting before 25. It also describes excessive tanning as a recognised dependence in some people, informally called tanorexia.[5] Wikipedia's sun tanning article adds that UVB-induced tan offers only a modest SPF of about 3.[1]

A 2007 study led by Katinka Jung, described in Wikipedia's article on sunless tanning, found DHA-treated skin formed substantially more free radicals under sunlight than untreated skin, and the article advises sun protection for at least a day after application. A fake tan itself offers no UV protection.[2]

lore.intro: Tanning oils and related accelerators are discussed in appearance circles as ways to get a deeper, glossier tan; the claims below are drawn from how the products are described in encyclopedic and regulatory coverage.[1][8]

claims.claim: Tanning oil makes you tan faster or deeper
Tan accelerators with tyrosine boost melanin production
A DHA oil gives a tan without sun
Tanning oils with little or no SPF are a normal part of sunbathing

timeline.event: Tanned skin becomes fashionable after Coco Chanel's Riviera tan.[1]
Jean Patou launches Huile de Chaldee, described as the first sun tan oil.[1]
Baby oil is widely used to increase tanning; Eva Wittgenstein finds DHA stains skin brown.[1][2]
Man-Tan, the first commercial DHA self-tanner, is released.[2]
Tanning beds reach the US market; SPF 15 sunscreens and standardised FDA labelling appear.[5][1]
Psoralen tanning activators are banned by health authorities.[1]
IARC review leads WHO to classify UV radiation as a Group 1 carcinogen.[5]
The FDA reclassifies tanning beds as moderate-risk devices with a black-box warning for under-18s.[5]
